A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Tensor Product Attention (TPA) and T6 research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

before.justification: v3 reports original FineWeb-Edu training and validation results, downstream benchmark evaluations, and rank and learning-rate ablations.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds measured decoding times and evaluations of third-order and non-contextual-B TPA variants.

M1.justification: The core TPA factorization and T6 architecture remain unchanged. v4 introduces FlashTPA decoding and a blocked Triton kernel with online softmax and partial-output accumulation (Section 4, Algorithms 1 and 3). This adds a concrete inference procedure beyond the general factorized computation already derived in v3 Appendix A.

E1.justification: The FineWeb-Edu corpus and nine downstream benchmarks are retained. v4 adds an empirical test scenario for single-token decoding with long KV caches, covering 4,096–524,288 tokens (Section 5.2). v3 Appendix A.8 discussed decoding costs analytically without these runtime evaluations.

E2.justification: v4 adds non-contextual-B TPA to the small- and medium-model comparisons in Tables 6–9; the existing non-contextual-A results are relocated and retained. MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA remain the external baseline families. The new timing comparison explicitly evaluates their FlashMHA, FlashMQA, FlashGQA, and FlashMLA implementations.

E3.justification: The new decoding protocol varies batch size and embedding dimension, using ranks (16,1,1), head dimension 64, and four GQA KV groups. Separately, v4 Appendix J.1 changes the stated medium-model maximum learning rate from 6e-4 to 3e-4 and minimum from 3e-5 to 6e-5. J.3 and Table 15 still identify 6e-4 as the default maximum, so the reported revision does not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds small- and medium-model third-order TPA evaluations (Tables 4–5) and comparisons of non-contextual A versus B factors (Tables 6–9). These test structural choices previously described but not evaluated this way. The original rank and learning-rate ablations remain in Appendix J.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, standard errors, or significance tests for its experiments. The added results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v4 adds decoding-time results in Figures 5, 7, and 8 and eight new benchmark rows for third-order and non-contextual-B variants. All retained per-task benchmark scores are unchanged. Two averages are corrected in v3 Table 13 versus v4 Table 19: MQA changes from 49.29 to 51.42, and TPA-KVonly from 49.93 to 52.15, without changes to their component scores.

T1.justification: v4 revises the vectorization definition and higher-order RoPE theorem and proof, replacing Rt ⊗ Idc with Idc ⊗ Rt^T for right multiplication under column-stacking (Theorem E.1, Appendix F.2). Appendix C also revises computational-cost reasoning to include value aggregation and an explicit condition for full-attention FLOP savings, beyond v3's looser efficiency discussion.

C1.justification: FlashTPA and its claimed speed advantage over optimized decoding baselines become a fourth main contribution. The abstract narrows T6's performance claim from exceeding baselines to surpassing or matching them. The contribution list also broadens the stated cache-reduction comparison to MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA, while retaining the core contextual-factorization and RoPE claims.

C2.justification: v4 expands the interpretation of computational savings, distinguishes memory-access benefits from FLOP counts, and adds qualifications about Triton versus CUDA implementations and the need for matched higher-order comparisons. It also introduces extensive speed interpretations in Appendix D.3. Some conflict with the plots: Figure 5 labels MQA purple and TPA red, with MQA faster at the longest contexts, contrary to the accompanying comparison.

D1.justification: v4 adds detailed decoding pseudocode, tensor shapes, rank-one cache conventions, kernel blocking, online-softmax updates, and partial-output layouts (Algorithms 1–3 and Appendix D). These substantially expand implementation information beyond v3's algebraic descriptions. Most optimizer and hardware details are retained or relocated; the learning-rate values are revised, and the T6 repository link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to FlashAttention-3, FlashMLA, and Triton to support its decoding implementation and comparisons. The existing positioning against attention variants, KV-cache compression, and static low-rank methods is largely retained. Moving related work to Appendix G and changing citation style do not constitute additional substantive changes.

P1.justification: Existing prose is extensively rewritten and reorganized. Attention unification, architecture recaps, RoPE background, related work, and training details move into dedicated appendices, while FlashTPA becomes a main-text section. Explanations of factorization, mathematical conventions, and computational costs are substantially reworked.

P2.justification: v4 adds two computation diagrams (Figures 2 and 6), three sets of decoding-time plots (Figures 5, 7, and 8), and third-order and factor-comparison tables (Tables 4–9). Existing non-contextual-A rows are regrouped into dedicated tables. The original figures are retained, mostly renumbered or relocated, while typography and page layout also change.

improvement.justification: v4 adds useful kernel details, variant experiments, and a repaired higher-order RoPE derivation. However, its new efficiency discussion misidentifies plotted methods and claims long-context advantages over MQA that Figure 5 contradicts: MQA's purple curve lies below TPA's red curve at the longest contexts. Appendix J.1 also conflicts with J.3 and Table 15 on the medium learning rate. These unresolved problems affect the new central contribution and reproducibility, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment despite the substantive gains.
